name: Australia
summary: A will can generally leave the estate to anyone, but each state and territory lets a court award provision to family and dependants who were left too little. Australia has trust law and the Hague Trusts Convention is in force. There is no private family foundation; only charitable structures exist.
family_claims: Each state and territory has a family provision regime, e.g. NSW Succession Act 2006 Ch 3; Vic Administration and Probate Act 1958 Pt IV; Qld Succession Act 1981 Pt 4; WA Family Provision Act 1972; SA Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1972 (now consolidated in the Succession Act 2023 (SA)); Tas Testators Family Maintenance Act 1912; ACT Family Provision Act 1969; NT Family Provision Act 1970. Eligible persons and the court's powers differ by state; claims can reach assets in a trust only in NSW through 'notional estate' orders.
foreign_law_note: No choice of law by nationality. Succession to land follows the law of the place where it lies; succession to movables follows the deceased's last domicile (common-law conflict rules), so a foreign domiciliary's movables are governed by foreign law, but Australian land and family provision claims on Australian-domiciled estates are not avoided.
trust_note: Convention in force for Australia since 1 Jan 1992 (ratified 17 Oct 1991). Trusts are governed by state Trusts/Trustee Acts and general law; foreign trusts are recognised. Trust income is taxed under the trust regime (Div 6 ITAA 1936), with special rules for non-resident trusts and the Foreign Resident CGT regime. There is no private foundation law; 'private ancillary funds' are charitable only.
open_questions: Confirm the 'notional estate' scope outside NSW and the exact family-provision statute section numbers per state.
